messages.author: 74f2e6fef4c447fd
messages.subject: Posteriors for derived parameters
parts:
Hi All,

I feel like I should know the answer to this question, but I don't.  I am wondering about the best way to calculate credible intervals for derived parameters from a model when using INLA.  For example, I have three populations of snakes.  I want to estimate body mass for each population given an average body length.  I have an ANCOVA, with a centered length covariate, an intercept to estimate mean mass and credible interval for population A, and two other estimates and credible intervals for differences between populations A and B, and A and C.  I understand that I just add the posterior means for differences between groups to the posterior mean of the intercept to get the posterior mean masses for populations B and C.  But how do I get a credible intervals for mean masses of populations B and population C, when they are derived from two sets of posteriors?  If I were doing this with MCMC, I'd calculate a derived mass for each population at each iteration to get a posterior for each population mass.  But what is the best way to get this using INLA?  Some code and output -- and question marks -- below.

###   make data  ###
n.groups <- 3; n.sample <- 30
n <- n.groups * n.sample
x <- rep(1:n.groups, rep(n.sample, n.groups)) 
pop <- factor(x, labels = c("Population A", "Population B", "Population C"))
length <- runif(n, 45, 70)
Xmat <- model.matrix(~ pop*length)
print(Xmat, dig = 2) 
beta.vec <- c(-250, 150, 200, 6, -3, -4)
lin.pred <- Xmat[,] %*% beta.vec
eps <- rnorm(n = n, mean = 0, sd = 10)
mass <- lin.pred + eps
dat <- data.frame(mass=mass, pop=pop, length=length)
dat$length <- scale(dat$length)
library(lattice); xyplot(mass ~ length | pop, data=dat)


###  inla model  ###
library(INLA)
form <- mass ~ pop + length
summary(res <- inla(formula=form, data=dat))


### output  ###
Fixed effects:      mean     sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant     mode kld
(Intercept)     103.7029 2.6876    98.3992 103.7078   108.9734 103.7175   0
popPopulation B -29.1395 3.8482   -36.6901 -29.1472   -21.5547 -29.1619   0
popPopulation C -29.5663 3.7750   -36.9742 -29.5736   -22.1265 -29.5874   0
length           23.5600 1.5984    20.4108  23.5611    26.6996  23.5634   0

Model hyperparameters:       mean    sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant   mode
Precision for the Gaussian 0.0047 7e-04     0.0035   0.0047     0.0061 0.0046


### means and credible intervals ###
Mean mass for population A is 103.7 (98.4, 109.0)
Mean mass for population B is 103.7 - 29.1 = 74.6 (?, ?)
Mean mass for population C is 103.7 - 29.6 = 74.1 (?, ?)

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Posteriors for derived parameters
parts:
If all you need are linear combinations of the latent variables (that looks like the case in your example) you can use the lincomb feature. See the FAQ on r-inla.org and the general documentation.

For more complex and/or nonlinear functionals, you can obtain posterior samples inla.posterior.sample() (which does direct MC sampling, not MCMC).

Finn

messages.author: 74f2e6fef4c447fd
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Posteriors for derived parameters
parts:
Here is the code for solution to example for anyone interested. Thanks again, Finn!


### Linear combinations - simple ANCOVA example
### Make data

n.groups <- 3
n.sample <- 30
n <- n.groups * n.sample
x <- rep(1:n.groups, rep(n.sample, n.groups)) 
pop <- factor(x, labels = c("Population A", "Population B",

"Population C")) ### Categorical factor
length <- runif(n, 45, 70) ### Continuous covariate

Xmat <- model.matrix(~ pop*length)
print(Xmat, dig = 2) 
beta.vec <- c(-250, 150, 200, 6, -3, -4)
lin.pred <- Xmat[,] %*% beta.vec
eps <- rnorm(n = n, mean = 0, sd = 10)
mass <- lin.pred + eps
dat <- data.frame(mass=mass, pop=pop, length=length)

dat$length <- scale(dat$length, scale=F) # note that length is centered
library(lattice); xyplot(mass ~ length | pop, data=dat) ### Plot of data


### simple ANCOVA model without linear combinations

library(INLA)
form <- mass ~ pop + length
summary(res <- inla(formula=form, data=dat))

### Create linear combinations to get posteriors for masses of Populations 
##### B and C at average length
### NOTE that NAMES of EFFECTS can be gleaned from fixed effects output of 
##### previous model. Just need to set the desired values for each effect.
lcPopB <- inla.make.lincomb("(Intercept)"=1, "popPopulation B"=1, 
             "popPopulation C"=0, length=0)
lcPopC <- inla.make.lincomb("(Intercept)"=1, "popPopulation B"=0, 
             "popPopulation C"=1, length=0)
lcAllPop <- c(lcPopB, lcPopC) ### Combine into a group
names(lcAllPop) <- c("lcPopB","lcPopC") ### MUST give unique names to each


### Rerun the model with the linear combinations
summary(res <- inla(formula=form, data=dat,
                    ### Add the linear combinations here
                    lincomb = lcAllPop,
                    ### Force noise variance to be essentially zero
                    control.family = list(initial=10, fixed=TRUE),
                    ### For higher accuracy
                    control.inla = list(lincomb.derived.only=FALSE)))


### Access summary of linear combinations
res$summary.lincomb


### Plot posteriors for mass of each population
yx <- data.frame(rbind(res$marginals.fixed$"(Intercept)", 
                       res$marginals.lincomb$lcPopB,
                       res$marginals.lincomb$lcPopC))
yx$poplab <- rep(c("Population A", "Population B",  "Population C"), 
                 each=nrow(res$marginals.lincomb$lcPopC))
xyplot(y~x|poplab, yx, scales=list(relation="free"), type="l",
       xlab="Posterior mass for each population", ylab="Density")


### Done
